belief/B-004:
Epsom salts prevent blossom-end rot.

Refuted

Epsom salts won't stop blossom-end rot. BER is a calcium-transport problem caused by uneven watering. A magnesium shortage doesn't cause it, and Epsom salts add magnesium, not calcium. Water evenly, mulch to buffer soil moisture, and soil-test before adding anything.

What is actually known

Blossom end rot is a localized calcium shortage in the fruit, driven by uneven water uptake. Calcium rides the transpiration stream, so erratic watering starves the fruit tip even when soil calcium is adequate. It is not a magnesium deficiency. Epsom salts add magnesium, not calcium, and the calcium is usually already in the soil, so they do nothing for BER. The levers are even watering and mulch; get a soil test before adding any nutrient.

belief/B-007:
You must rotate every crop to new ground every single year.

Contested

You don't have to move every crop every single year by rule. What matters is keeping each crop family out of the same soil long enough to starve its diseases, commonly three to five years. Rotating yearly is a good habit. It isn't a law, and perennials like asparagus and rhubarb stay put for years.

What is actually known

Rotation works by starving a pathogen out of the soil, so the right interval depends on how long that pathogen survives, and for many diseases that cannot be stated precisely. Extension advice is to keep a crop family out of the same soil for three to five years; clubroot of the mustard family can survive seven years, bacterial spot needs at least two years without a host, and soil-dwelling soft-rot bacteria are not managed by rotation at all. belief/B-009:
A layer of gravel or pot shards at the bottom of a container improves drainage.

Contested

The old "never put gravel in the bottom of a pot" rule is overstated. A 2025 controlled test found a bottom layer usually drained soil-less mixes better and almost never made things worse, though in loam-based compost it mostly made no difference. It's one study and it grew no plants, so treat a layer as an option. It isn't a fix. If you use one, a thicker layer of coarse sand did best.

What is actually known

This one is contested. The popular "it's a myth" answer rests on the perched water table. Water held in the fine mix by capillarity was predicted not to cross into a coarse layer, so a gravel bottom would raise the saturated zone and hold more water. A 2025 controlled experiment, using the potting mixes and drainage materials home gardeners actually use, found the opposite. A drainage layer almost always reduced or did not change the water a container held, and almost never increased it. In soil-less coir mixes every layer drained the mix; in loam-based compost most made no difference. Thicker layers did more, and 60 mm of coarse sand worked best across every mix. The study grew no plants, so whether a given plant benefits is still open.

belief/B-011:
Marigolds repel most garden pests and protect the whole garden.

Marigolds don't protect the whole garden. Their best-known trick is underground. A dense planting of the right kind, grown at least two months before your crop, suppresses root-knot nematodes. What is actually known

Marigolds are not a garden-wide shield. Their best-established effect is on root-knot and some other nematodes in the soil. A dense stand of the right Tagetes, planted at least two months before the crop, suppresses them. Whether that is through the root compound alpha-terthienyl or because marigold is not a host is not settled. belief/B-012:
Watering plants in the midday sun scorches the leaves

Watering plants in the midday sun scorches the leaves (water droplets focus sunlight like lenses).

Refuted

Watering in the midday sun won't scorch your leaves. Droplets don't focus sunlight on ordinary leaves. Water whenever the plant needs it, and aim at the soil and keep the leaves dry, because wet foliage invites fungal disease. Morning or evening watering just loses less to evaporation than the middle of the day.

What is actually known

Water droplets on a leaf do not focus the sun into a burn. On smooth, hairless leaves, sunlit drops of every shape caused no burn damage in a controlled optics study, and wet foliage is not prone to sunburn. The rare exception is a leaf whose water-repellent hairs hold a round drop just above the surface, as on a floating fern. There the drop can focus light and, out of contact with the leaf, no longer cools it. Hundreds of studies of leaf scorch have never pinned it on midday watering. What timing does affect is efficiency. Watering in the heat of the day loses more to evaporation than morning or evening watering, though evening watering can help fungal disease take hold. That is one more reason to put the water on the soil and keep it off the foliage.

belief/B-015:
Mixing sand into clay soil improves its drainage.

Refuted

Don't add sand to clay to "loosen" it. In the amounts anyone actually adds, the clay fills the gaps and you get a denser, worse-draining mix. Work in compost and mulch instead; organic matter is what builds the structure that drains.

What is actually known

A modest amount of sand in clay does the opposite of what is intended. The fine clay fills the gaps between the sand grains, giving a dense, poorly-draining mix closer to concrete than to loam. To actually shift the texture you would need sand in huge volumes (over half by volume), which is impractical for a bed. What does open clay is organic matter. Compost and mulch build aggregate structure and the pore space that drains. (Whether a gravel layer helps a container drain is a separate and more equivocal case; here the mechanism, clay filling the pore space between the sand grains, is well established.)

belief/B-016:
Household vinegar is an effective weed killer.

Contested

Vinegar only burns the parts of a weed it touches, so it works on tiny seedlings, but bigger and perennial weeds grow back from the roots. It also harms any plant it hits, crops included. The strong "horticultural" kinds can burn skin and eyes. Use it for seedlings in paving cracks. It isn't a garden weed killer.

What is actually known

Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid, a contact herbicide. It burns only the parts of a plant it touches, fastest in bright sun, and gives excellent control of very small annual broadleaf weeds. It does not move to the roots, so larger and perennial weeds can regrow a week or so later, and it is non-selective, injuring any plant it lands on. Stronger products are more dangerous to the person using them. At 11% acetic acid or more, vinegar can burn skin and cause severe eye injury, and 20-30% formulations call for protective gear. It is most useful for weeds in gravel and on patios and sidewalks. It is not a general weed killer.

belief/B-019:
Compost tea (or manure tea) greatly boosts growth and suppresses plant disease.

Contested

Compost tea isn't the tonic or disease cure it's sold as. The effects in the field are patchy, and aerated teas have no documented disease protection. Additives like molasses can grow E. coli and Salmonella, so keep it off food crops unless you're sure of the method. Spreading the compost itself as mulch is the better bet.

What is actually known

Compost tea, made by steeping mature compost in water, is a source of nutrients, but its disease claims are weak. Batches vary widely; results that look good in the laboratory are more variable in the field; aerated teas have no scientifically documented effect as pathogen suppressors, while non-aerated teas show a trend to reduce how often foliar diseases appear, though not how severe they are. There is a real food-safety downside too. Sugars and other additives commonly put into aerated teas can feed E. coli and Salmonella, so unless the brewing method keeps human pathogens down, extension advice is to save the tea for plants you will not eat. Using the compost itself as mulch is simpler, and composted mulch has documented disease suppression of its own.

That is the opposite of a deterrent, and a trap crop only helps if you then deal with the beetles on it. rule/R-001:
Corn needs a block of at least three short rows side by side for good kernel set

Corn needs a block of at least three short rows side by side for good kernel set, and four rows is better.

Well established A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, the planting fails. The planner won’t allow it.

How it works

Maize is wind-pollinated and protandrous (each plant sheds its pollen before its own silks are ready). Tassels shed pollen that must land on the silks of neighboring plants. In a single row much of the pollen blows out of the row, and each silk it misses is one missing kernel.

What to do about it

Plant corn in a block of several short rows rather than one long row; four rows is best. For a small patch, shake the stalks gently while the tassels shed pollen, or dust a cut tassel over the silks, every few days. Or leave corn out and give the beans a trellis.

How much it matters: A single row gives ears with blank areas where kernels did not form.

Zones encode average annual minimum winter temperature, which governs whether a woody perennial survives to spring. It is the wrong quantity for an annual, which never sees winter. rule/R-115:
A seedling raised indoors is set out gradually, not all at once

Do not harvest asparagus at all the first year after planting crowns. When harvest begins (the second or third spring, depending on the source you follow), keep it short. Pick for about two weeks in the first harvest year, no more than a month, then let every later spear grow out. From the fourth year on, harvest can run eight to ten weeks. After harvest ends, let the spears grow into ferns and leave them standing, because the ferns are what feed the crown for next year.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

Every spear is drawn from energy stored in the crown, and the ferns are what refill that store. The fern's photosynthesis is banked underground to produce the following year's spears. A young planting is still expanding its root storage system, so cutting its spears removes the shoots that would have become ferns, and excessive removal of spears weakens the plants. Restraint in the establishment years is what builds a crown strong enough to bear a full harvest for decades.

What to do about it

Year one after planting crowns: harvest nothing and let everything fern out. In the first year you do harvest, pick for about two weeks only, a month at most, then stop. From the fourth year on, harvest from first spears through May or June, about eight to ten weeks. Every year, once harvest ends, let the remaining spears develop into ferns and take care of them; they are next year's crop being banked.

How much it matters: No figure is given beyond the durations the sources state (no harvest year one; about two weeks, at most a month, in the first harvest year; eight to ten weeks from year four). The sources say over-harvest of a young bed weakens the plants and give no yield numbers. Because the harvest calendar is entirely the gardener's choice, the rule only advises.

rule/R-135:
On a new June-bearing strawberry planting, remove every blossom for the whole first season

On a new June-bearing strawberry planting, remove every blossom for the whole first season. Check weekly and pinch or cut them off; flowering stops by early July. Letting first-year flowers set fruit reduces plant growth, runner production, and the size of next year's crop. Everbearing and day-neutral types are handled differently. Remove blossoms only for the first stretch after planting (about four to six weeks, or until early July), then let them fruit. The first berries come in August and keep coming until frost.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

A first-year plant that ripens fruit spends on berries the resources that would otherwise build the root system, leaf canopy and runners (daughter plants) that make up next year's bed; letting the flowers develop into berries reduces plant growth, runner production and the size of next year's crop, while removing them directs the plant's resources into a large root system and a healthy plant. June-bearers crop once a year, so the whole first season is given to establishment; everbearing and day-neutral types keep flowering, so only the establishment window is sacrificed and later flowers are allowed to fruit.

What to do about it

June-bearing: pinch or cut off all blossoms weekly through the first growing season. Everbearing or day-neutral: remove blossoms for the first four to six weeks after planting, or until early July, then allow the plants to fruit.

How much it matters: No figure is stated. The sources give a direction with no magnitude. First-year fruiting means a smaller next-year crop, fewer runners and weaker plants; removal builds the root system and canopy. Because deblossoming a young planting is the gardener's weekly choice, the rule only advises.

rule/R-136:
Grapes fruit on new shoots that grow from last season's canes

Grapes fruit on new shoots that grow from last season's canes, and only a few well-placed canes are kept. Prune hard every dormant season, in late winter after the coldest weather but before the buds swell. Removing about 80 to 90 percent of the previous year's growth is normal and necessary. Under-pruning is the common mistake and leaves a tangled vine with fewer flower buds and small, poor-quality fruit.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

Fruit forms only on shoots arising from last season's canes, so a vine left unpruned piles up old wood that no longer fruits while the crop crowds onto too many buds. Cutting back 80 to 90 percent of last year's growth concentrates the vine into a small number of well-placed, productive canes; prune too little and too many buds remain, so the vine over-produces small, poor fruit and becomes a tangled mass.

What to do about it

Prune while the vine is fully dormant, after the coldest part of winter, before the buds begin to swell, around February to March. Remove roughly 80 to 90 percent of the previous year's wood, keeping a few strong, well-placed canes (and renewal spurs) according to your training system. Do not under-prune.

How much it matters: The one figure, about 80 to 90 percent of last year's wood removed at dormant pruning, is stated by both sources (Illinois "80 to 90%", Maryland "90 percent"). The direction of the consequence (fewer flower buds, small poor-quality fruit, and a biennial bearing pattern) is sourced; no other magnitude is claimed. Because pruning is the gardener's annual dormant-season choice, the rule only advises.

rule/R-137:
Tree fruits differ in whether a lone tree can set a crop

Tree fruits differ in whether a lone tree can set a crop. Apples and most European pears are self-unfruitful. One cultivar alone will not set a normal crop, so plant at least two different cultivars whose bloom periods overlap. For apple, a flowering crabapple in bloom at the same time also works. European plums are partially to entirely self-fruitful, and a second European plum cultivar makes fruit set reliable. Japanese and hybrid plums will not cross-pollinate them. Peaches and sour cherries are self-fruitful and may be planted alone. Partner trees must stand near each other. The published distances are within 50 to 100 feet, and 300 feet at most.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

A self-unfruitful tree will not set a normal crop from its own pollen or the pollen of another tree of the same cultivar; it needs pollen from a genetically different, compatible cultivar, carried by bees while both trees are in bloom. That is why the partner must be a different cultivar, must bloom at the same time, and must stand within a bee's working range. It is also why a self-fruitful species like peach or sour cherry, whose own pollen sets fruit, bears alone.

What to do about it

Check the pollination requirement before buying. For apple and pear, plant two different cultivars with overlapping bloom. Early- and late-blooming cultivars may miss each other, and for apple a flowering crabapple that blooms at the same time also serves. For European plum, pair with a second European plum cultivar. A Japanese or hybrid plum won't do. Site partner trees close together, within 50 to 100 feet where you can and within 300 feet at most. A peach or sour cherry needs no partner.

How much it matters: No figure is added here. The magnitude is the sources': a self-unfruitful tree alone 'will not set a normal crop' (apples set at most a small crop on their own pollen), and the two planting distances (within 50 to 100 feet; within 300 feet) are both published figures, both carried, neither chosen. Because cultivar choice at planting is the gardener's own decision and the app cannot see what grows in neighboring yards, the rule only advises.

rule/R-139:
Elderberries must be cooked before eating. Raw or unripe berries

Elderberries must be cooked before eating. Raw or unripe berries, and all leaves, stems and roots, are toxic; only fully ripe, cooked berries are safe.

Well established A person has checked it against its sources. This one is about eating safely, not how the plant grows. The planner suggests it.

How it works

The plant holds cyanogenic glycosides, highest in the unripe fruit, leaves, stems and roots and lower in ripe fruit. Eaten raw they release cyanide in the gut and cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; cooking ripe berries drives off and inactivates the compound, which is why cooked elderberry (syrup, wine, jelly) is a traditional food while the raw plant is not.

What to do about it

Eat only fully ripe berries, and only after cooking. Never eat raw berries, unripe green berries, or any leaves, stems or roots.

rule/R-140:
Some plants come as separate male and female plants

Some plants come as separate male and female plants, and you need one of each for fruit.

As recorded: Dioecious species need both a male and a female plant to set fruit.

Well established A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, you lose real yield. The planner warns you.

How it works

A dioecious species carries male and female flowers on separate plants. Some plants make only pollen, others only fruit. A lone plant, or a planting that is all one sex, sets no fruit at all, because there is no pollen to reach the female flowers. Fruit needs at least one male plant near the fruiting females. This is a different mechanism from the single-locus self-incompatibility of apple and pear. There a plant has both sexes and rejects only its own pollen; here whole plants are one sex. So it is a separate rule and does not widen that one.

What to do about it

Plant at least one male alongside the female fruiting plant(s). A single plant, or several of the same sex, will never fruit. A few named cultivars are self-fertile and need no separate male; if you grow one of those, one plant is enough.

How much it matters: Categorical, with no dose involved. Without a pollen source a dioecious female sets no fruit. The floor is two plants (one male, one female). The planner can't see a plant's sex any more than it can see which cultivar you planted, so it states the requirement without claiming you've met it.

rule/R-141:
A self-incompatible pome fruit's pollen partner has to bloom at the same time and make viable pollen

A self-incompatible pome fruit's pollen partner has to bloom at the same time and make viable pollen. A triploid apple cannot be the pollen source, and a second tree of the same variety is not a second cultivar.

Well established A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

Cross-pollination only works while both cultivars' flowers are open together, so their bloom periods must overlap: early with mid, or mid with late. Early and late can miss each other entirely. A normal cultivar makes viable pollen; a triploid apple, with three sets of chromosomes instead of two, makes little or none and cannot fertilize a partner even though it needs one itself. Two plants of a single variety, including a colored sport of it, are genetically identical, so they reject each other's pollen exactly as a lone tree does.

What to do about it

Pick the second cultivar so its bloom overlaps the first, and do not rely on a triploid apple (Gravenstein, Winesap, Mutsu or Crispin, Jonagold) for pollen. Grow one only beside two other cultivars that pollinate each other. An ornamental crabapple that blooms at the same time will pollinate any apple. Two strains of one variety do not count as two cultivars. The partner does not have to share the bed. Within 50 to 100 feet is close enough for the bees, so a neighbor's tree of a different variety counts. For apple, a crabapple in bloom at the same time does too.

rule/R-142:
A bed watered for its vegetables is too wet for its Mediterranean herbs

A bed watered for its vegetables is too wet for its Mediterranean herbs. Tomato, pepper, cucumber and basil want the soil kept steadily moist, about an inch a week; rosemary, sage, thyme, oregano and lavender want it to dry between waterings. One bed gets one regime, and whichever way it is watered, half the planting suffers.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

The vegetables' yield and fruit quality depend on steady soil moisture, so the bed is irrigated to keep it moist. In that same soil the herbs' root zone never dries, oxygen is starved and the roots and stem base rot, the failure the herb rule describes. Watered for the herbs instead, the vegetables run short at fruit set.

What to do about it

Give the herbs their own bed or container beside the vegetables, with sharp drainage, as a dry herb bed. If they must share, put the herbs at the highest, driest edge and water at the base of the vegetables only.

How much it matters: No figure is stated. The two regimes are each well documented; the conflict is the inference that one bed cannot hold both, and the rule only advises, because a gardener can water by hand at the base.

rule/R-143:
A border of a more attractive cucurbit (blue hubbard

A border of a more attractive cucurbit (blue hubbard, a winter squash), planted a week or two before the crop and kept unbroken around it draws striped cucumber beetles to the edge, where they are dealt with, so most of the beetles, and the bacterial wilt they carry, never reach the cucumbers, melons or summer squash inside.

As recorded: A border of a more attractive cucurbit (blue hubbard, a Cucurbita maxima), planted a week or two before the crop and kept unbroken around it draws striped cucumber beetles to the edge, where they are dealt with, so most of the beetles, and the bacterial wilt they carry, never reach the cucumbers, melons or summer squash inside.

How it works

Striped cucumber beetles prefer Cucurbita maxima to C. pepo and C. moschata, and they arrive in one early flush from whatever direction they overwintered. A perimeter of the preferred host intercepts that flush on every side and concentrates the beetles on plants the gardener can treat or strip, so the unsprayed center sees far fewer beetles and far less of the wilt bacterium they transmit. The trap concentrates the beetles and does not kill them. The beetles in the border must be removed, or the ring feeds the crop instead of protecting it.

What to do about it

Plant hubbard a week or two ahead of the crop in an unbroken ring around it, at no wider than the crop's own row spacing. Check the ring when the beetles arrive and deal with them there, by hand, under a cover, or with whatever control you choose. Keep checking the center. Do not use a border that bacterial wilt kills quickly.

How much it matters: Connecticut trials on summer squash: over 94% of the beetles were on the perimeter plants, beetle numbers on the unsprayed center fell by up to 95%, and spraying the border cut vine borer on the center by 88%. rule/R-144:
Ground that just carried cereal rye or a sorghum cover crop is a poor seedbed for small seeds for a few weeks

Ground that just carried cereal rye or a sorghum cover crop is a poor seedbed for small seeds for a few weeks. As the residue breaks down it releases chemicals that stop small seeds germinating, and the smaller the seed the worse it fares; transplants and big seeds largely shrug it off.

How it works

Rye and sorghum roots and residue release allelochemicals (benzoxazinoids from rye, sorgoleone from sorghum) that persist in the surface soil for weeks after the cover is killed. A small seed sown into that layer has little reserve to push through the inhibition; a large seed or a transplant is already past the germination window.

What to do about it

Wait about two weeks after killing rye and about four after sorghum before sowing small seeds, water an inch to leach the surface, or plant transplants. Big seeds and transplants can go in sooner.

How much it matters: Georgia saw very poor carrot germination after a sorghum-family cover and asks for four weeks and an inch of water; Iowa asks for ten to fourteen days after rye before corn and says susceptibility runs with seed size. No garden figure is given; the two lead times are the sources' own, and the rye figure rests on corn and transplant timings plus the seed-size principle. rule/R-145:
Limed ground is the wrong ground for the next potato crop

Limed ground is the wrong ground for the next potato crop, because common scab worsens as soil pH rises and lime raises it.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. If you skip this, it still grows, just less well. The planner suggests it.

How it works

Common scab (Streptomyces scabies) infects young tubers through the lenticels and is favored as soil goes less acid; at about pH 5.2 and below it is largely suppressed. Lime raises pH and its effect lasts years, so ground limed for a crop that wants sweet soil carries a scab-prone pH into the seasons that follow.

This ground has been limed, and potatoes want it sour. Scab is skin-deep and the tubers still eat, but where it has been a problem, put the potatoes on ground you have not limed, choose a scab-resistant variety, keep the soil evenly moist for the four to nine weeks after planting while the tubers set, and never lime or add wood ash where potatoes are going next. A later pH reading at or below about 5.2 on this ground would quiet this. rule/R-147:
Do not plant alliums in ground that held alliums within 4 years

rule/R-180:
A cover buys cool-season crops a week or two at the ends of the season.

As recorded: A row cover, low tunnel or cold frame lets cool-season crops go in earlier in spring and keep growing later in autumn: about a week earlier under a row cover, and about two weeks at each end under a low tunnel or a cold frame.

Soil warmed by the sun by day is the heat source at night; a covering low to the ground traps that heat around the plants on calm, clear nights, keeping them a few degrees above the open air through the light frosts at each end of the season.

rule/R-189:
We check a soil pH against a plant's range only when it was measured in water, the way the ranges are written

We check a soil pH against a plant's range only when it was measured in water, the way the ranges are written. A reading in calcium chloride is kept and shown, and never converted.

As recorded: Milpa reads every soil pH range and threshold it checks plants against as water pH. A pH a lab measured in calcium chloride, or in another salt solution, is recorded and shown with its method. It is never compared with those numbers, and never converted to water pH by a fixed amount.

Promising A person has checked it against its sources. Read against a range written in water pH, a pH measured another way can flag a plant that’s fine or miss one that isn’t. The planner keeps that reading and checks no plant against it.

How it works

A pH read in a calcium chloride solution is commonly 0.5 to 1.0 unit lower than the same soil read in water, by an amount that changes with the soil's type and salt content, so a range written in water pH cannot be compared with it or reached by adding a fixed number.

When this applies to a garden, Milpa says: This reading wasn't taken in water, or the report doesn't say how it was, and the ranges here are in water pH. Readings in calcium chloride usually run half a unit to a unit lower than in water, and the gap moves with your soil's salt, so we keep the reading without checking plants against it.

What to do about it

Ask your lab for the pH in water. Many labs measure both, and some print a water figure they worked out themselves; that one counts, because it is the lab's. Enter the water pH and the plants are checked against it.
